CausalChain: Chronic inflammation (HBV/HCV/metabolic stress) -> Increased IL‐6 secretion -> Persistent IL‐6/STAT3 activation -> Epigenetic silencing of SOCS3 (loss of negative feedback) -> Uncontrolled STAT3 activation -> Upregulation of lipid synthesis genes -> Metabolic reprogramming and enhanced energy supply -> Promotion of cancer stem cell characteristics, tumor growth and drug resistance
Hypothesis: In HCC, chronic inflammatory conditions induce persistent IL‐6/STAT3 signaling that epigenetically silences SOCS3, thus establishing a feed-forward loop that reprograms hepatocyte lipid metabolism to favor tumor initiation, progression, and resistance to therapy. Targeting both STAT3 activity and the epigenetic modifications of its negative regulators could therefore offer a novel therapeutic strategy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by complex interactions in the tumor microenvironment, with the IL‐6/STAT3 signaling cascade playing a pivotal role in disease initiation and progression. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis wherein chronic hepatic inflammation, due to viral infections or metabolic insults, leads to sustained IL‐6 stimulation and persistent STAT3 activation. This continuous signaling drives an epigenetic silencing of negative regulators such as SOCS3, effectively removing the brake on the pathway. The unrestrained STAT3 activation, in turn, is hypothesized to reprogram hepatocyte metabolism toward enhanced lipid biosynthesis, thereby supplying the energy and building blocks needed for tumor cell growth, drug resistance, and the maintenance of liver cancer stem cells. Therapeutically, combinatorial strategies targeting both the IL‐6/STAT3 axis and the epigenetic machinery governing negative feedback may offer improved efficacy in suppressing HCC progression.
